questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211825/assets/b5b4d260ad31b6c4efc3f7314e98df8b422f8d92f0f21fa436334c4b15d88a67.png)

Consider a sample of size $n=80$ from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the proportion of those in the sample with the characteristic is $\overset{^}{\,p}=0.7,$ find a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of individuals having this characteristic.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05,$ where $Z∼N(0,1),$ as shown in the diagram above.*
questions.worked_solution:
Since $n=80$ and $\overset{^}{\,p}=0.75,$ we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=80\cdot 0.7=56>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=80\cdot (1-0.7)=24>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.05}=1.645.
$$

Therefore, a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.7\pm 1.645\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.7(1-0.7)}{80}} \\  & 0.7\pm 0.084\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
A survey conducted by a sports magazine on a random sample of $125$ students from various U.S. universities reported that $40$ respondents love soccer. Find a $99%$ confidence interval for the national proportion of college students who love soccer. 

*Hint: Given a random variable $Z∼N(0,1),$ the table below shows the $z$-scores ${z}_{p}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{p})=p$ for some particular values of $p.$*

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's interpret the data:

- the population consists of all college students in the US,

- some of the students surveyed love soccer, and some don't,

- the size of the random sample is $n=125,$ and

- the proportion of students from the sample who love soccer can be found as follows:

$$
\overset{^}{p\,}=\frac{40}{125}=0.32
$$

Now, we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=125\cdot 0.32=40>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=125\cdot (1-0.32)=85>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation: 

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

 

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.005}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.005})=0.005,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211825/assets/f5e154855d4a4f18fb81d522873fb29c11fd7c9543ffebdeac0f15672c7e72b2.png)

From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.005}=2.576:$  

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

Therefore, a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.32\pm 2.576\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.32(1-0.32)}{125}} \\  & 0.32\pm 0.107\end{aligned}
$$

questions.raw_html:
3.Finding Confidence Intervals for Population Proportions In Context?

A poll of 800 randomly selected U.S. Internet subscribers reveals that only 560 of those interviewed are satisfied with their current internet provider. Find a 99% confidence interval for the proportion of all U.S. internet users that are satisfied with their current internet providers.

Hint: Given a random variable Z∼N(0,1), the table below shows the z-scores zp such that P(Z>zp)=p for some particular values of p.

p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
zp 1.282 1.645 1.960 2.326 2.576
H

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211825/assets/8f0308aa9c39034a938a5f5c63ca049ab21a47fddc20b592d660a70254990ff0.png)

Consider a sample of size $n=75$ from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the proportion of those in the sample with the characteristic is $\overset{^}{\,p}=0.4,$ find a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of individuals having this characteristic.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>2.576)=0.005,$ where $Z∼N(0,1),$ as shown in the diagram above.*
questions.worked_solution:
Since $n=75$ and $\overset{^}{\,p}=0.4,$ we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=75\cdot 0.4=30>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=75\cdot (1-0.4)=45>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>2.576)=0.005.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.005}=2.576.
$$

Therefore, a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.4\pm 2.576\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.4(1-0.4)}{75}} \\  & 0.4\pm 0.146\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider a sample of size $n=160$ from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that $5%$ of the sample has the characteristic, find a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion of individuals having this characteristic.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$*
questions.worked_solution:
Since $n=160$ and $\overset{^}{\,p}=5%=0.05,$ we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=160\cdot 0.05=8>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=160\cdot (1-0.05)=152>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.90=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.05}=1.645.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211825/assets/b5b4d260ad31b6c4efc3f7314e98df8b422f8d92f0f21fa436334c4b15d88a67.png)

Therefore, a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.05\pm 1.645\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.05(1-0.05)}{160}} \\  & 0.05\pm 0.028\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let's interpret the data:

- the population consists of all college students in the US,

- some of the students surveyed love soccer, and some don't,

- the size of the random sample is $n=125,$ and

- the proportion of students from the sample who love soccer can be found as follows:

$$
\overset{^}{p\,}=\frac{40}{125}=0.32
$$

Now, we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=125\cdot 0.32=40>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=125\cdot (1-0.32)=85>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation: 

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

 

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.005}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.005})=0.005,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211825/assets/f5e154855d4a4f18fb81d522873fb29c11fd7c9543ffebdeac0f15672c7e72b2.png)

From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.005}=2.576:$  

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

Therefore, a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.32\pm 2.576\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.32(1-0.32)}{125}} \\  & 0.32\pm 0.107\end{aligned}
$$

Since $n=160$ and $\overset{^}{\,p}=5%=0.05,$ we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=160\cdot 0.05=8>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=160\cdot (1-0.05)=152>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.90=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.05}=1.645.
$$

Therefore, a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.05\pm 1.645\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.05(1-0.05)}{160}} \\  & 0.05\pm 0.028\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Since $n=80$ and $\overset{^}{\,p}=0.75,$ we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=80\cdot 0.7=56>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=80\cdot (1-0.7)=24>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.9=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.05}=1.645.
$$

Therefore, a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.7\pm 1.645\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.7(1-0.7)}{80}} \\  & 0.7\pm 0.084\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Consider a sample of size n=80 from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the proportion of those in the sample with the characteristic is p^=0.7, find a 90% confidence interval for the population proportion p of individuals having this characteristic.

Hint: Use the fact that P(Z>1.645)=0.05, where Z∼N(0,1), as shown in the diagram above.

a
0.7±0.051
b
0.9±0.205
c
0.7±0.126
d
0.7±0.084
e
0.9±0.152
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since n=80 and p^=0.75, we have that

  • np^=80⋅0.7=56>5, and

  • n(1−p^)=80⋅(1−0.7)=24>5.

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

p^−pp^(1−p^)/n|∼N(0,1),

where

  • p^ is the sample proportion,

  • p is the population proportion, and

  • n is the sample size.

Given a value α between 0 and 1, the corresponding [100(1−α)]% confidence interval for the population proportion p of the original distribution can be written as

p^±zα/2⋅p^(1−p^)n,

where P(Z>zα/2)=α2 and Z∼N(0,1).

We are interested in finding a 90% confidence interval. So, we have

α=1−0.9=0.1⟹α2=0.05.

We are given that P(Z>1.645)=0.05. As a result,

zα/2=z0.05=1.645.

Therefore, a 90% confidence interval for the population proportion p is the following:

0.7±1.645⋅0.7(1−0.7)800.7±0.084

solution.reasoning: The 90% normal confidence interval is \hat p\pm1.645\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}=0.7\pm1.645\sqrt{0.7(0.3)/80}\approx0.7\pm0.084, so option d is mathematically correct. The sample has 56 successes and 24 failures, supporting the normal approximation. No captured Math Academy answer or grading evidence establishes its key.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
A survey conducted by a sports magazine on a random sample of $125$ students from various U.S. universities reported that $40$ respondents love soccer. Find a $99%$ confidence interval for the national proportion of college students who love soccer. 

*Hint: Given a random variable $Z∼N(0,1),$ the table below shows the $z$-scores ${z}_{p}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{p})=p$ for some particular values of $p.$*

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |
question.worked_solution:
First, let's interpret the data:

- the population consists of all college students in the US,

- some of the students surveyed love soccer, and some don't,

- the size of the random sample is $n=125,$ and

- the proportion of students from the sample who love soccer can be found as follows:

$$
\overset{^}{p\,}=\frac{40}{125}=0.32
$$

Now, we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=125\cdot 0.32=40>5,$ and

Question 2
?

A survey conducted by a sports magazine on a random sample of 125 students from various U.S. universities reported that 40 respondents love soccer. Find a 99% confidence interval for the national proportion of college students who love soccer.

Hint: Given a random variable Z∼N(0,1), the table below shows the z-scores zp such that P(Z>zp)=p for some particular values of p.

p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
zp 1.282 1.645 1.960 2.326 2.576
a
0.32±0.054
b
0.64±0.17
c
0.32±0.107
d
0.40±0.576
e
0.16±0.17
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's interpret the data:

  • the population consists of all college students in the US,

  • some of the students surveyed love soccer, and some don't,

  • the size of the random sample is n=125, and

  • the proportion of students from the sample who love soccer can be found as follows: p^=40125=0.32

Now, we have that

  • np^=125⋅0.32=40>5, and

  • n(1−p^)=125⋅(1−0.32)=85>5.

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

p^−pp^(1−p^)/n|∼N(0,1),

where

  • p^ is the sample proportion,

  • p is the population proportion, and

  • n is the sample size.

Given a value α between 0 and 1, the corresponding [100(1−α)]% confidence interval for the population proportion p of the original distribution can be written as

p^±zα/2⋅p^(1−p^)n,

where P(Z>zα/2)=α2 and Z∼N(0,1).

We are interested in finding a 99% confidence interval. So, we have

α=1−0.99=0.01⟹α2=0.005.

We also need to find the z-score value z0.005 such that P(Z>z0.005)=0.005, where Z∼N(0,1).

From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that z0.005=2.576:

p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
zp 1.282 1.645 1.960 2.326 2.576

Therefore, a 99% confidence interval for the population proportion p is the following:

0.32±2.576⋅0.32(1−0.32)1250.32±0.107

question.html:
Question 2
?

A survey conducted by a sports magazine on a random sample of 125 students from various U.S. universities reported that 40 respondents love soccer. Find a 99% confidence interval for the national proportion of college students who love soccer.

Hint: Given a random variable Z∼N(0,1), the table below shows the z-scores zp such that P(Z>zp)=p for some particular values of p.

p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
zp 1.282 1.645 1.960 2.326 2.576
a
0.32±0.054
b
0.64±0.17
c
0.32±0.107
d
0.40±0.576
e
0.16±0.17
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's interpret the data:

  • the population consists of all college students in the US,

  • some of the students surveyed love soccer, and some don't,

  • the size of the random sample is n=125, and

  • the proportion of students from the sample who love soccer can be found as follows: p^=40125=0.32

Now, we have that

  • np^=125⋅0.32=40>5, and

  • n(1−p^)=125⋅(1−0.32)=85>5.

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

p^−pp^(1−p^)/n|∼N(0,1),

where

  • p^ is the sample proportion,

  • p is the population proportion, and

  • n is the sample size.

Given a value α between 0 and 1, the corresponding [100(1−α)]% confidence interval for the population proportion p of the original distribution can be written as

p^±zα/2⋅p^(1−p^)n,

where P(Z>zα/2)=α2 and Z∼N(0,1).

We are interested in finding a 99% confidence interval. So, we have

α=1−0.99=0.01⟹α2=0.005.

We also need to find the z-score value z0.005 such that P(Z>z0.005)=0.005, where Z∼N(0,1).

From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that z0.005=2.576:

p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
zp 1.282 1.645 1.960 2.326 2.576

Therefore, a 99% confidence interval for the population proportion p is the following:

0.32±2.576⋅0.32(1−0.32)1250.32±0.107

solution.reasoning: The sample proportion is 40/125=0.32. A 99% interval leaves probability 0.005 in each tail, so z=2.576. Thus the interval is 0.32\pm2.576\sqrt{0.32(0.68)/125}\approx0.32\pm0.107, matching option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem:
A survey conducted by a sports magazine on a random sample of $125$ students from various U.S. universities reported that $40$ respondents love soccer. Find a $99%$ confidence interval for the national proportion of college students who love soccer. 

*Hint: Given a random variable $Z∼N(0,1),$ the table below shows the $z$-scores ${z}_{p}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{p})=p$ for some particular values of $p.$*

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's interpret the data:

- the population consists of all college students in the US,

- some of the students surveyed love soccer, and some don't,

- the size of the random sample is $n=125,$ and

- the proportion of students from the sample who love soccer can be found as follows:

$$
\overset{^}{p\,}=\frac{40}{125}=0.32
$$

Now, we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=125\cdot 0.32=40>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=125\cdot (1-0.32)=85>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation: 

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

 

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.005}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.005})=0.005,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211825/assets/f5e154855d4a4f18fb81d522873fb29c11fd7c9543ffebdeac0f15672c7e72b2.png)

From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.005}=2.576:$  

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

Therefore, a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.32\pm 2.576\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.32(1-0.32)}{125}} \\  & 0.32\pm 0.107\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:

*Hint: Given a random variable $Z∼N(0,1),$ the table below shows the $z$-scores ${z}_{p}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{p})=p$ for some particular values of $p.$*

- some internet subscribers are satisfied with their current internet provider, and some aren't,

- the size of the random sample is $n=800,$ and

- the proportion of Internet subscribers from the sample who are satisfied with their current internet provider is found as follows:

$$
\overset{^}{p\,}=\frac{560}{800}=0.7
$$

Now, we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=800\cdot 0.7=560>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=800\cdot (1-0.7)=240>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation: 

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

 

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.005}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.005})=0.005,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211825/assets/f5e154855d4a4f18fb81d522873fb29c11fd7c9543ffebdeac0f15672c7e72b2.png)

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |

Therefore, a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0,7\pm 2.576\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.7(1-0.7)}{800}} \\  & 0.7\pm 0.042\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

A poll of 800 randomly selected U.S. Internet subscribers reveals that only 560 of those interviewed are satisfied with their current internet provider. Find a 99% confidence interval for the proportion of all U.S. internet users that are satisfied with their current internet providers.

Hint: Given a random variable Z∼N(0,1), the table below shows the z-scores zp such that P(Z>zp)=p for some particular values of p.

p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
zp 1.282 1.645 1.960 2.326 2.576
a
0.35±0.021
b
0.35±0.042
c
0.7±0.084
d
0.7±0.042
e
0.7±0.021
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's interpret the data:

  • the population consists of all U.S. internet users,

  • some internet subscribers are satisfied with their current internet provider, and some aren't,

  • the size of the random sample is n=800, and

  • the proportion of Internet subscribers from the sample who are satisfied with their current internet provider is found as follows: p^=560800=0.7

Now, we have that

  • np^=800⋅0.7=560>5, and

  • n(1−p^)=800⋅(1−0.7)=240>5.

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

p^−pp^(1−p^)/n|∼N(0,1),

where

  • p^ is the sample proportion,

  • p is the population proportion, and

  • n is the sample size.

Given a value α between 0 and 1, the corresponding [100(1−α)]% confidence interval for the population proportion p of the original distribution can be written as

p^±zα/2⋅p^(1−p^)n,

where P(Z>zα/2)=α2 and Z∼N(0,1).

We are interested in finding a 99% confidence interval. So, we have

α=1−0.99=0.01⟹α2=0.005.

We also need to find the z-score value z0.005 such that P(Z>z0.005)=0.005, where Z∼N(0,1).

From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that z0.005=2.576:

p 0.100 0.050 0.025 0.010 0.005
zp 1.282 1.645 1.960 2.326 2.576

Therefore, a 99% confidence interval for the population proportion p is the following:

0,7±2.576⋅0.7(1−0.7)8000.7±0.042

First, let's interpret the data:

- the population consists of all U.S. internet users,

- some internet subscribers are satisfied with their current internet provider, and some aren't,

- the size of the random sample is $n=800,$ and

- the proportion of Internet subscribers from the sample who are satisfied with their current internet provider is found as follows:

$$
\overset{^}{p\,}=\frac{560}{800}=0.7
$$

Now, we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=800\cdot 0.7=560>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=800\cdot (1-0.7)=240>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation: 

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

 

We also need to find the $z$-score value ${z}_{0.005}$ such that $P(Z>{z}_{0.005})=0.005,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211825/assets/f5e154855d4a4f18fb81d522873fb29c11fd7c9543ffebdeac0f15672c7e72b2.png)

From the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that ${z}_{0.005}=2.576:$  

| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${z}_{p}$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |

Therefore, a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0,7\pm 2.576\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.7(1-0.7)}{800}} \\  & 0.7\pm 0.042\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211825/assets/8f0308aa9c39034a938a5f5c63ca049ab21a47fddc20b592d660a70254990ff0.png)

Consider a sample of size $n=75$ from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the proportion of those in the sample with the characteristic is $\overset{^}{\,p}=0.4,$ find a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of individuals having this characteristic.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>2.576)=0.005,$ where $Z∼N(0,1),$ as shown in the diagram above.*
question.worked_solution:
Since $n=75$ and $\overset{^}{\,p}=0.4,$ we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=75\cdot 0.4=30>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=75\cdot (1-0.4)=45>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>2.576)=0.005.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.005}=2.576.
$$

Therefore, a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.4\pm 2.576\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.4(1-0.4)}{75}} \\  & 0.4\pm 0.146\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Since $n=75$ and $\overset{^}{\,p}=0.4,$ we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=75\cdot 0.4=30>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=75\cdot (1-0.4)=45>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $99%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.99=0.01\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.005.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>2.576)=0.005.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.005}=2.576.
$$

Therefore, a $99%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.4\pm 2.576\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.4(1-0.4)}{75}} \\  & 0.4\pm 0.146\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Consider a sample of size n=75 from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the proportion of those in the sample with the characteristic is p^=0.4, find a 99% confidence interval for the population proportion p of individuals having this characteristic.

Hint: Use the fact that P(Z>2.576)=0.005, where Z∼N(0,1), as shown in the diagram above.

a
0.4±0.132
b
0.6±0.132
c
0.4±0.146
d
0.4±0.111
e
0.6±0.146
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since n=75 and p^=0.4, we have that

  • np^=75⋅0.4=30>5, and

  • n(1−p^)=75⋅(1−0.4)=45>5.

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

p^−pp^(1−p^)/n|∼N(0,1),

where

  • p^ is the sample proportion,

  • p is the population proportion, and

  • n is the sample size.

Given a value α between 0 and 1, the corresponding [100(1−α)]% confidence interval for the population proportion p of the original distribution can be written as

p^±zα/2⋅p^(1−p^)n,

where P(Z>zα/2)=α2 and Z∼N(0,1).

We are interested in finding a 99% confidence interval. So, we have

α=1−0.99=0.01⟹α2=0.005.

We are given that P(Z>2.576)=0.005. As a result,

zα/2=z0.005=2.576.

Therefore, a 99% confidence interval for the population proportion p is the following:

0.4±2.576⋅0.4(1−0.4)750.4±0.146

solution.reasoning: The 99% confidence interval is \hat p\pm2.576\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}=0.4\pm2.576\sqrt{0.4(0.6)/75}\approx0.4\pm0.146, matching option c. The sample contains 30 successes and 45 failures, supporting the normal approximation. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider a sample of size $n=160$ from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that $5%$ of the sample has the characteristic, find a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion of individuals having this characteristic.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$*
question.worked_solution:
Since $n=160$ and $\overset{^}{\,p}=5%=0.05,$ we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=160\cdot 0.05=8>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=160\cdot (1-0.05)=152>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.90=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.05}=1.645.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211825/assets/b5b4d260ad31b6c4efc3f7314e98df8b422f8d92f0f21fa436334c4b15d88a67.png)

Therefore, a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.05\pm 1.645\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.05(1-0.05)}{160}} \\  & 0.05\pm 0.028\end{aligned}
$$

Hint: Use the fact that P(Z>1.645)=0.05, where Z∼N(0,1).

a

p^−pp^(1−p^)/n|∼N(0,1),

  • p is the population proportion, and

p^±zα/2⋅p^(1−p^)n,

where P(Z>zα/2)=α2 and Z∼N(0,1).

We are interested in finding a 90% confidence interval. So, we have

α=1−0.90=0.1⟹α2=0.05.

We are given that P(Z>1.645)=0.05. As a result,

zα/2=z0.05=1.645.

Therefore, a 90% confidence interval for the population proportion p is the following:

0.05±1.645⋅0.05(1−0.05)1600.05±0.028

question.html:
Question 5
?

Consider a sample of size n=160 from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that 5% of the sample has the characteristic, find a 90% confidence interval for the population proportion of individuals having this characteristic.

Hint: Use the fact that P(Z>1.645)=0.05, where Z∼N(0,1).

a
0.95±0.028
b
0.95±0.034
c
0.05±0.044
d
0.05±0.028
e
0.05±0.034
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since n=160 and p^=5%=0.05, we have that

  • np^=160⋅0.05=8>5, and

  • n(1−p^)=160⋅(1−0.05)=152>5.

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

p^−pp^(1−p^)/n|∼N(0,1),

where

  • p^ is the sample proportion,

  • p is the population proportion, and

  • n is the sample size.

Given a value α between 0 and 1, the corresponding [100(1−α)]% confidence interval for the population proportion p of the original distribution can be written as

p^±zα/2⋅p^(1−p^)n,

where P(Z>zα/2)=α2 and Z∼N(0,1).

We are interested in finding a 90% confidence interval. So, we have

α=1−0.90=0.1⟹α2=0.05.

We are given that P(Z>1.645)=0.05. As a result,

zα/2=z0.05=1.645.

Therefore, a 90% confidence interval for the population proportion p is the following:

0.05±1.645⋅0.05(1−0.05)1600.05±0.028

solution.reasoning: Using the indicated normal approximation, the interval is 0.05\pm1.645\sqrt{0.05(0.95)/160}\approx0.05\pm0.028, matching option d. This is an approximate interval; only 8 sampled individuals have the characteristic. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
Consider a sample of size $n=160$ from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that $5%$ of the sample has the characteristic, find a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion of individuals having this characteristic.

*Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05,$ where $Z∼N(0,1).$*
feedback.worked_solution:
Since $n=160$ and $\overset{^}{\,p}=5%=0.05,$ we have that

- $n\overset{^}{\,p}=160\cdot 0.05=8>5,$ and

- $n(1-\overset{^}{\,p})=160\cdot (1-0.05)=152>5.$

As a result, we may use the following normal approximation:

$$
\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}-p}{\sqrt{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})/n}}∼N(0,1),
$$

where 

- $\,\overset{^}{\,p}$ is the sample proportion,

- $p$ is the population proportion, and

- $n$ is the sample size.

Given a value $\alpha $ between $0$ and $1,$ the corresponding $[100(1-\alpha )]%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}\pm {z}_{\alpha /2}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{\overset{^}{\,p}(1-\overset{^}{\,p})}{n}},
$$

where $P(Z>{z}_{\alpha /2})=\frac{\alpha }{2}$ and $Z∼N(0,1).$

We are interested in finding a $90%$ confidence interval. So, we have 

$$
\alpha =1-0.90=0.1\,⟹\,\frac{\alpha }{2}=0.05.
$$

We are given that $P(Z>1.645)=0.05.$ As a result, 

$$
{z}_{\alpha /2}={z}_{0.05}=1.645.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14211825/assets/b5b4d260ad31b6c4efc3f7314e98df8b422f8d92f0f21fa436334c4b15d88a67.png)

Therefore, a $90%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 0.05\pm 1.645\cdot \sqrt{\frac{0.05(1-0.05)}{160}} \\  & 0.05\pm 0.028\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Olivia and Harper are musicians. In the previous season, the decimal proportion of Olivia’s performances that were solos was $0.55,$ while $40%$ of Harper’s performances were solos. 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. Less than half of Olivia's performances were solos.

II. More than half of Harper's performances were solos.

III. Olivia had a greater percentage of solo performances compared to Harper.
questions.html:
1.Identifying True Statements in Context?

Olivia and Harper are musicians. In the previous season, the decimal proportion of Olivia’s performances that were solos was 0.55, while 40% of Harper’s performances were solos.

Which of the following statements are true?

  1. Less than half of Olivia's performances were solos.
  2. More than half of Harper's performances were solos.
  3. Olivia had a greater percentage of solo performances compared to Harper.
E
Wed, Oct 14th @ 11:26 AM|Elapsed: 1:19Correct

choices.html: I and II only
I only
III only
II only
None

evidence.solution_quote: Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

questions.worked_solution:
Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, since 

$$
0.55>0.5,
$$

more than half of Olivia's performances were solos.

- Statement II is false. Notice that 

$$
40%<50%.
$$

So, less than half of Harper's performances were solos.

- Statement III is true. We can compare $0.55$ and $40%$ by converting the decimal into a percent. 

To do this, we multiply it by $100:$

$$
0.55\times 100=55%
$$

Since $55%>40%,$ Olivia had a **greater** percentage of solo performances compared to Harper.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

questions.problem:
Which of the following are natural numbers?

I. $-1$

II. $0$

III. $11$
questions.html:
2.Classifying Numbers as Natural?

Which of the following are natural numbers?

  1. −1
  2. 0
  3. 11
M
Wed, Oct 14th @ 11:26 AM|Elapsed: 0:46Correct

choices.html: I only
II only
III only
II and III only
I and II only

evidence.solution_quote: Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.worked_solution:
The natural numbers consist of all positive whole numbers.

$$
1,\,2,\,3,\,4,\,5,…
$$

Of the given numbers, $11$ is a natural number, but $-1$ and $0$ are not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.worked_solution:
We count the number of rectangles. We see that there are $3$ rectangles.

We count the total number of shapes. We see that there are $6$ shapes in total.

So the ratio of rectangles to total shapes is $3:6.$

We can simplify this ratio by dividing both numbers in a ratio by $3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,3 &  & : & \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,6 &  \\ \,\,↓÷\,\,3 &  &  &  & \,\,\,↓÷\,\,3 &  \\ \,\,1 &  & : &  & \,\,\,2 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the ratio of rectangles to the total shapes is $1:2.$

questions.worked_solution:
A number is divisible by $9$ if the sum of its digits is divisible by $9.$

- The sum of the digits of $7\,050\,113$ is

$$
7+0+5+0+1+1+3=17,
$$

which is *not* divisible by $9.$ So, $7\,050\,113$ is *not* divisible by $9.$

- The sum of the digits of $5\,119\,232$ is

$$
5+1+1+9+2+3+2=23,
$$

which is *not* divisible by $9.$ So, $5\,119\,232$ is *not* divisible by $9.$

- The sum of the digits of $14\,624\,100$ is

$$
1+4+6+2+4+1+0+0=18,
$$

which is divisible by $9.$ So, $14\,624\,100$ is divisible by $9.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "llI only."

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: The height of a cone is increasing at a rate of $5\,\text{in}/\text{min}.$ The diameter of the cone is always $3$ times its height. At what rate is the cone's volume increasing when its height is $6\,\text{in}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the cone and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=5\,\text{in}\text{/min},
$$

and we need to find $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=6\,\text{in}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

We're told that the diameter is $3$ times the height. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =3h \\ 2r & =3h \\ r & =\frac{3}{2}h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{3}{2}h)}^{2}\cdot h=\frac{3}{4}\pi {h}^{3}.
$$

Now that we have an equation relating just $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{4}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{9}{4}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{9}{4}\pi (6)^{2}(5) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =405\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: The radius of the base of a cone is decreasing at a rate of $4\,\text{m}/\text{h}.$ The height of the cone is always half its radius. At what rate is the cone's volume decreasing when the radius of its base is $12\,\text{m}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the cone and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}=-4\,\text{m}/\text{h},
$$

and we need to find $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=12\,\text{m}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $r.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $h$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $h$ in terms of $r.$

We're told that the height of the cone is half its radius. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =\frac{r}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}\cdot (\frac{r}{2})=\frac{1}{6}\pi {r}^{3}.
$$

Now that we have an equation relating just $v$ and $r,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{6}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi (12)^{2}(-4) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =-288\pi \,{\text{m}}^{3}/\text{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the cone's volume is decreasing at a rate of $288\pi \,{\text{m}}^{3}/\text{h}.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
The height of a cone is decreasing at a rate of $6\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.$ The diameter of the cone is always $4$ times its height. Find the rate of the cone's volume decrease when the height is $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{cm}.$ Do not round the answer. 

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of decrease is positive.

The volume is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the cone and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-6\,\text{cm}/\text{s},
$$

and we need to find $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{cm}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

We're told that the diameter is $4$ times the height. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =4h \\ 2r & =4h \\ r & =2h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {(2h)}^{2}\cdot h=\frac{4}{3}\pi {h}^{3}.
$$

Now that we have an equation relating just $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}(-6) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =-6\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the cone's volume is decreasing at a rate of $6\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: The height of a cone is increasing at a rate of $24\,\text{ft}/\text{h}.$ The radius of the cone is always $\frac{3}{5}$ times its height. At what rate is the cone's volume increasing when its height is $6.25\,\text{ft}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the cone and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=24\,\text{ft}/\text{h},
$$

and we need to find $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=6.25\,\text{ft}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

We're told that the radius of the cone is $\frac{3}{5}$ times its height. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\frac{3}{5}h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{3}{5}h)}^{2}\cdot h=\frac{3}{25}\pi {h}^{3}.
$$

Now that we have an equation relating just $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{25}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{9}{25}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{9}{25}\pi (6.25)^{2}(24) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =337.5\pi \,{\text{ft}}^{3}/\text{h}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
The height of a cone is increasing at a rate of $4\,\text{in}/\text{s}.$ The diameter of the cone is always $4$ times its height. Find the rate of the cone's volume increase when height is $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{in}.$ Do not round the answer.

The volume is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{in}}^{3}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the cone and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=4\,\text{in}\text{/s},
$$

and we need to find $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=\frac{1}{2}\,\text{in}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

We're told that the diameter is $4$ times the height. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =4h \\ 2r & =4h \\ r & =2h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {(2h)}^{2}\cdot h=\frac{4}{3}\pi {h}^{3}.
$$

Now that we have an equation relating just $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi {(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}(4) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the cone's volume is increasing at a rate of $4\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{s}.$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212195/assets/a3623402e5d5df9339f1a3bb615c92ff5fcff9ae8d96c3630c5cb847a3038eda.png)

Water is leaking out of a cone-shaped container so that the volume of the water decreases at a rate of $12\,{\text{in}}^{3}\text{/min}.$ The height of the container is three times its base radius. Find the rate of decrease of the radius of the water's surface when the radius is $6\,\text{in}.$ Do not round the answer.

*Hint*: Assume that the rate of decrease is positive.

The radius is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} $\text{in}/\text{min}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the conical volume of water and $r$ be the radius of its surface. Both of these quantities, as well as the water's volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-12\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{min},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=6\,\text{in}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we want the rate of change, which is $r.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $h$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $h$ in terms of $r.$

We're told that the height is always three times its base radius. So, we have $h=3r.$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}(3r) \\  & =\pi {r}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $r,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =3\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values and solving for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-12 & =3\pi (6)^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\ -12 & =108\pi \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{9\pi }\,\text{in}/\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the water's surface decreases at a rate of $\frac{1}{9\pi }\,\text{in}/\text{min}.$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: The volume of a cone is decreasing at a rate of $14\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{h}.$ The radius of the cone is always $7$ times its height. At what rate is the height of the cone decreasing when its height is $2\,\text{in}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the cone and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-14\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{h},
$$

and we need to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=2\,\text{in}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

We're told that the radius of the cone is $7$ times its height. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =7h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi (7h)^{2}\cdot h=\frac{49}{3}\pi {h}^{3}.
$$

Now that we have an equation relating just $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =49\pi {h}^{2}(\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values and solving for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-14\pi  & =49\pi (2)^{2}(\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{14}\,\text{in/h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the height of the cone is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{1}{14}\,\text{in}/\text{h}.$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
The volume of a cone is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{4}\pi \,{\text{m}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ The diameter of the cone is always one third of its height.  Find the rate of the cone's height increase when the  height is $6\,\text{m}.$ Do not round the answer.

The height is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} $\text{ m/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the cone and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{3}{4}\pi \,{\text{m}}^{3}\text{/s},
$$

and we need to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=6\,\text{m}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

We're told that the diameter is one third of the height. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{1}{3}h \\ 2r & =\frac{1}{3}h \\ r & =\frac{1}{6}h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{1}{6}h)}^{2}h=\frac{1}{108}\pi {h}^{3}.
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{1}{36}\pi {h}^{2}(\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}).
$$

Finally, substituting the known values and solving for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}\pi  & =\frac{1}{36}\pi (6)^{2}(\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the cone's height is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{4}\text{ m/s}.$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: The volume of a cone is decreasing at a rate of $72\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{s}.$ The radius of the cone is always equal to its height. At what rate is the height of the cone decreasing when its height is $6\,\text{in}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the cone and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-72\,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we need to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=6\,\text{in}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

We're told that the radius of the cone is equal to its height. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi (h)^{2}\cdot h=\frac{1}{3}\pi {h}^{3}.
$$

Now that we have an equation relating just $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\pi {h}^{2}(\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values and solving for $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-72 & =\pi (6)^{2}(\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{2}{\pi }\,\text{in/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the height of the cone is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{2}{\pi }\,\text{in}/\text{s}.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212195/assets/8036801735554767a33bdee0ff96a95d7e44bc3f97bacb396ec0de6d38f4aafc.png)

A cone is being filled with ice-cream at a rate of $4\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ The height of the cone is always three times its base radius. At what rate is the radius of the ice cream volume increasing when the radius is $1\,\text{cm}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's call $h$ the height of the ice cream volume and $r$ the radius of its base. Both of these quantities, as well as the volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=1\,\text{cm}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $h$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $h$ in terms of $r.$

We're told that the height is always three times its base diameter. So, we have $h=3r.$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}(3r) \\  & =\pi {r}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $r,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =3\pi {r}^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values and solving for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =3\pi (1)^{2}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\ 4 & =3\pi \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{4}{3\pi }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212195/assets/cf9fda11d138a5227307070d52fc0a27ce9decc35c91efbb026b89d4507f2ce7.png)

A beverage is pumped into a conical dispenser at a constant rate of  $19.6\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min}.$ The mouth of the tank is $70\,\text{cm}$ in diameter and the height of the tank is $40\,\text{cm}.$ How fast is the beverage level increasing when the volume of the beverage in the dispenser is $12.25\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}?$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the tank. Let's call $H=40\,\text{cm}$ the height of the tank, and $R=\frac{70}{2}=35\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the solution level. We call $h$ the solution level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the solution. Both of these quantities, and the solution volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=19.6\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $v=12.25\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the tank and the solution must be similar. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{35}{40} \\ r & =\frac{7h}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{7h}{8})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{49}{192}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{49}{192}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{49}{64}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the rate at which the level of the beverage in the dispenser is changing when $v=12.25\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ We can compute the value of $h$ at this moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}12.25\pi  & =\frac{49}{192}\pi {h}^{3} \\ {h}^{3} & =48 \\ h & =2\sqrt[3]{6}\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug in the known values into the formula for $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}19.6\pi  & =\frac{49}{64}\pi (2\sqrt[3]{6})^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 19.6\pi  & =\frac{49\sqrt[3]{36}}{16}\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & ≈1.94\,\text{cm}/\text{min}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the solution level is increasing at a rate of approximately $1.94\,\text{cm}/\text{min}.$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212195/assets/a9c0d78ce05859db77dcc1e5198596a1a02c798c607ba9c4ff78e6fe1362b113.png)

The height of a conical cup is $6\text{ cm}$ and the opening radius is $2\text{ cm}.$ Water leaks out of the bottom at the rate of $2\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ If the water level is $3\,\text{cm}$ at a particular moment, how fast is the water level decreasing at that moment?
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the cup. Let's call $H=6\,\text{cm}$ the height of the cup, and $R=2\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the water level. We call $h$ the water level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the water. Both of these quantities, and the water volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=3\,\text{cm}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the cup and the water must be similar. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{2}{6} \\ r & =\frac{h}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{h}{3})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{27}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{27}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{9}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug in the known values, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =\frac{1}{9}\pi ({3}^{2})\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ -2 & =\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{2}{\pi }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water level is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{2}{\pi }\,\text{cm/s}.$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212195/assets/8676d9a562d254a1194502c5a45368d5345f81aee3a066c28acc87cb1f33812c.png)

The height of an ice cream cone is $12\,\text{cm}$ and the radius at the top of the cone is $2\,\text{cm}.$ Ice cream is leaking from a small hole at the bottom at a rate of $2\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min}.$ If the ice cream level is $6\,\text{cm}$ at a particular moment, how fast is the ice cream level decreasing at that moment?
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the cone. Let's call $H=12\,\text{cm}$ the height of the cone, and $R=2\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the ice cream level. We call $h$ the height of the ice cream in the cone and $r$ the radius of the ice cream top surface. Both of these quantities, and the ice cream volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min},
$$

and we want to find the rate of change of the ice cream level $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $h=6\,\text{cm}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of the ice cream:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cone and the ice cream part of the cone must be similar. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{2}{12} \\ r & =\frac{h}{6}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{h}{6})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{108}\pi {h}^{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{108}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{36}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the rate of change of the ice cream level in the cone when $h=6\,\text{cm}.$ We can compute the value of $h$ at this moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\pi  & =\frac{1}{36}\pi ({6}^{2})\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-2\,\text{cm/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the height of the ice cream is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/min}.$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212195/assets/7732722fc875e8cf13482394990baa0b5f8306a8151fca934491bb12dd181d9e.png)

A  $10\,\text{cm}$ tall funnel containing water is being drained at a constant rate of  $10\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ The mouth of the funnel is $12\,\text{cm}$ in diameter. How fast is the water level dropping when there is $15\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}$ of water remaining in the funnel?
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the funnel. Let's call $H=10\,\text{cm}$ the height of the funnel, and $R=\frac{12}{2}=6\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the water level. We call $h$ the water level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the water. Both of these quantities, and the water volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-10\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $v=15\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the funnel and the water must be similar. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{6}{10} \\ r & =\frac{3h}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{3h}{5})}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{3}{25}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{25}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{9}{25}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the rate at which the level of water in the funnel is changing when $v=15\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ We can compute the value of $h$ at this moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}15\pi  & =\frac{3}{25}\pi {h}^{3} \\ {h}^{3} & =125 \\ h & =5\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug in the known values into the formula for $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-10 & =\frac{9}{25}\pi ({5}^{2})\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ -10 & =9\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{10}{9\pi }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water level is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{10}{9\pi }\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212195/assets/561e9e9bd41dddff575a95ed619d2ff3b91a48e0845960a6265c7c7cb1dc04fe.png)

A  $50\,\text{cm}$ beverage dispenser is being emptied at a constant rate of  $16\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min}.$ The mouth of the dispenser is $50\,\text{cm}$ in radius. How fast is the beverage level dropping when there is $576\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}$ of beverage remaining in the funnel?
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the funnel. Let's call $H=50\,\text{cm}$ the height of the funnel, and $R=50\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the top. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the water level. We call $h$ the water level's height and $r$ the radius of the cone formed by the water. Both of these quantities, and the water volume $v,$ change with time. In particular, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-16\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$ when $v=576\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$

We need to find a relation between $h$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $v.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the funnel and the water must be similar. Therefore, we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{50}{50} \\ r & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(h)}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{3}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find the rate at which the level of water in the funnel is changing when $v=576\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ We can compute the value of $h$ at this moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}576\pi  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {h}^{3} \\ {h}^{3} & =1\,728 \\ h & =12\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug in the known values into the formula for $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-16\pi  & =\pi (12)^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ -16 & =144\pi \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{1}{9}\,\text{cm}/\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the beverage level is decreasing at a rate of $\frac{1}{9}\,\text{cm}/\text{min}.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212195/assets/01d6575ff056e7f99075597547583b4c648fbe6ad462d38a5d5fd76b8c73a564.png)

A conical container has a height of $8\,\text{cm},$ and the radius at the bottom of the container is $4\,\text{cm}.$ Batter is being poured into the container. If the level of the batter in the container is increasing at a rate of $\frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{cm/s}$, find the rate at which the volume of the batter is increasing when the radius of the batter surface is $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}.$ Do not round the answer.

The volume of batter is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's consider the dimensions of the container. Let's call $H=8\,\text{cm}$ the height of the conical container, and $R=4\,\text{cm}$ its radius at the bottom. These quantities are fixed and do not change with time.

Now, let's consider the batter level. We call $h$ the distance from the top of the container to the batter surface, $r$ the radius of the cone at the surface of the batter, and $v$ the volume of the empty space in the container. All of these quantities change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-\frac{4}{\pi }\,\text{cm}/\text{s},
$$

which is negative because the distance from the top of the container to the batter surface decreases as we pour the batter into the container.

We want to know $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}.$

We need to find a relation between $v$ and the variable for which we know the rate of change, which is $h.$ This is given by the formula for the volume of a cone:

$$
v=\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}h.
$$

Before we differentiate the equation with respect to time, note that $r$ also appears in the formula. So, we need to simplify the formula by writing $r$ in terms of $h.$

Note that the cones formed by the container and the batter must be similar. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{r}{h} & =\frac{R}{H} \\ \frac{r}{h} & =\frac{4}{8} \\ r & =\frac{h}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the volume formula as

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {(\frac{h}{2})}^{2}h \\ v & =\frac{1}{12}\pi {h}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now that we have an equation relating $v$ and $h,$ we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}v & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{12}\pi {h}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{4}\pi {h}^{2}\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We want to know $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=\frac{3}{2}\,\text{cm}.$ We can compute the value of $h$ at this moment as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & =\frac{h}{2} \\ h & =3\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{1}{4}\pi (3)^{2}(-\frac{4}{\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} & =-9\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of batter is increasing at a rate of $9\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$
