Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{the origin}.$

Hence, to insure that ${e}^{at}\to 0,$ we require $a<0.$

Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{the origin}.$

Hence, to insure that ${e}^{at}\to 0,$ we require $a<0.$

Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{infinity}.$

Hence, to insure that ${e}^{at}\to \infty ,$ we require $a>0.$

feedback.worked_solution:
Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{infinity}.$

Hence, to insure that ${e}^{at}\to \infty ,$ we require $a>0.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)=10+x+y$ given that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical points in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=2\lambda x \\ 1=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{2\lambda } \\ y=\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
y=x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),\,(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ | $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $10+\sqrt{2}$ | $10-\sqrt{2}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),$ and its minimum value is $10-\sqrt{2}.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: A rectangular box without a lid has a surface area of $48{\text{ cm}}^{2}.$ Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum possible volume of the box.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,y$, and $z$ be the box's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
2xz+2yz+xy=48.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=2xz+2yz+xy.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=48
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2z+y,2z+x,2x+2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}yz=\lambda (2z+y) \\ xz=\lambda (2z+x) \\ xy=\lambda (2x+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}xyz=\lambda x(2z+y) \\ xyz=\lambda y(2z+x) \\ xyz=\lambda z(2x+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $xyz=0,$ which contradicts the constraints. Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2z+y) & =y(2z+x) \\ 2xz+xy & =2yz+xy \\ xz & =yz\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z\ne 0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $x=y=2z.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2xz+2yz+xy & =48 \\ 4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =48 \\ 12{z}^{2} & =48 \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(4,4,2),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(4,4,2)=4\cdot 4\cdot 2=32\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2,5.5) & =2\cdot 2\cdot 5.5 \\  & =22 \\  & <f(4,4,2).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, determine the maximum product of three positive numbers given that the sum of their squares is $108.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be three positive numbers. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=108.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=108
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}yz=2\lambda x \\ xz=2\lambda y \\ xy=2\lambda z\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}xyz=2\lambda {x}^{2} \\ xyz=2\lambda {y}^{2} \\ xyz=2\lambda {z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =108 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2} & =36 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(6,6,6),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(6,6,6)=6\cdot 6\cdot 6=216.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10,2,2) & =10\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =40 \\  & <f(6,6,6).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}$ given that $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 16.$ 

*Hint: The critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<16$ is $(0,0).$*
questions.worked_solution:
We are given that the critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region's interior is $(0,0).$

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=16
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4x,-6y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨8x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}4x=8\lambda x \\ -6y=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(1-2\lambda )=0 \\ y(3+\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,y=\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,\pm 4).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,x=\pm 2,\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm 2,0).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm 4),\,(\pm 2,0),\,(0,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,\pm 4)$ | $(\pm 2,0)$ | $(0,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $-48$ | $8$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,\pm 4),$ and its minimum value is $-48.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-4y$ given that $2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 4.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-4⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=4
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-4⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2x=4\lambda x \\ -4=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(1-2\lambda )=0 \\ \lambda y=-2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4\,⇒\,y=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,\pm 2).$

- Assuming $\lambda =\frac{1}{2}$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies 

$$
\frac{1}{2}y=-2\,⇒\,y=-4.
$$

 
Then, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+(-4)^{2}=4\,⇒\,{x}^{2}=-6\end{aligned}
$$

which has no solutions.

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm 2).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,2)$ | $(0,-2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-8$ | $8$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,2),$ and its minimum value is $-8.$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical points in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=2\lambda x \\ 1=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{2\lambda } \\ y=\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
y=x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),\,(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ | $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $10+\sqrt{2}$ | $10-\sqrt{2}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),$ and its minimum value is $10-\sqrt{2}.$

Question 1

Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function f(x,y)=10+x+y given that x2+y2≤1.

a
 10
b
 10−3
c
 10+2
d
 10
e
 10−2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving ∇f=0, as follows:

⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=⟨0,0⟩⟨1,1⟩=⟨0,0⟩

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical points in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of f(x,y) subject to the constraint g(x,y)=x2+y2=1.

Since f(x,y) is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, f(x,y) reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint.

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y)g(x,y)=1

We start by solving the first equation:

∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y)⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=λ⟨gx(x,y),gy(x,y)⟩⟨1,1⟩=λ⟨2x,2y⟩

Notice that we cannot have λ=0 since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming λ≠0, we have the following:

{1=2λx1=2λy⇒{x=12λy=12λ⇒x=y

Substituting y=x into the condition g(x,y)=1, we get

x2+y2=1x2+x2=12x2=1x2=12x=±12.

As a result, y=x=±12.

Therefore, f has possible extreme values at the points

(22,22),(−22,−22).

We evaluate f at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

(x,y) (22,22) (−22,−22)
f(x,y) 10+2 10−2

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at (−22,−22), and its minimum value is 10−2.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let $x,y$, and $z$ be the box's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
2xz+2yz+xy=48.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=2xz+2yz+xy.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=48
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2z+y,2z+x,2x+2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}yz=\lambda (2z+y) \\ xz=\lambda (2z+x) \\ xy=\lambda (2x+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}xyz=\lambda x(2z+y) \\ xyz=\lambda y(2z+x) \\ xyz=\lambda z(2x+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $xyz=0,$ which contradicts the constraints. Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2z+y) & =y(2z+x) \\ 2xz+xy & =2yz+xy \\ xz & =yz\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z\ne 0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $x=y=2z.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2xz+2yz+xy & =48 \\ 4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =48 \\ 12{z}^{2} & =48 \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(4,4,2),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(4,4,2)=4\cdot 4\cdot 2=32\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2z+y,2z+x,2x+2y⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\{\begin{aligned}yz=\lambda (2z+y) \\ xz=\lambda (2z+x) \\ xy=\lambda (2x+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

\{\begin{aligned}xyz=\lambda x(2z+y) \\ xyz=\lambda y(2z+x) \\ xyz=\lambda z(2x+2y)\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}x(2z+y) & =y(2z+x) \\ 2xz+xy & =2yz+xy \\ xz & =yz\end{aligned}

Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be three positive numbers. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=108.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=108
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}yz=2\lambda x \\ xz=2\lambda y \\ xy=2\lambda z\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}xyz=2\lambda {x}^{2} \\ xyz=2\lambda {y}^{2} \\ xyz=2\lambda {z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =108 \\ 3{x}^{2} & =108 \\ {x}^{2} & =36 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(6,6,6),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(6,6,6)=6\cdot 6\cdot 6=216.
$$

$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We are given that the critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region's interior is $(0,0).$

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=16
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4x,-6y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨8x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}4x=8\lambda x \\ -6y=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(1-2\lambda )=0 \\ y(3+\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,y=\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,\pm 4).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,x=\pm 2,\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm 2,0).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm 4),\,(\pm 2,0),\,(0,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,\pm 4)$ | $(\pm 2,0)$ | $(0,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $-48$ | $8$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,\pm 4),$ and its minimum value is $-48.$

judgments.reasoning: The earlier answer 10−√2 (option e) was graded Correct and agrees with the worked solution. There are no interior critical points. On the boundary, Lagrange multipliers give x=y=±1/√2; evaluating f yields 10±√2, so the minimum is 10−√2.

The earlier answer, 32 cm³ (option a), agrees with MA's worked solution. The captured submission was instead 24 cm³ (option b), so its Incorrect grade is consistent. Lagrange multipliers give x=y=2z; the surface constraint then yields z=2 and x=y=4, giving volume 32 cm³. AM–GM establishes the global bound: (xy)(2xz)(2yz)≤16³, hence xyz≤32. MA's final comparison with one other point alone does not prove global maximality, but its answer is correct.

The earlier answer 216 (option a) was graded Correct and matches MA's worked solution. The Lagrange equations yield xyz=2λx²=2λy²=2λz²; positivity implies x=y=z=6, giving product 216. AM–GM proves global maximality: x²y²z²≤36³, hence xyz≤216. MA's comparison with one other point alone is insufficient to prove a global maximum, but its answer is correct.

The earlier answer −48 (option d) agrees with MA's worked solution. The captured submission was −24 (option a), so its Incorrect grade is consistent. Lagrange multipliers on the boundary give candidates (0,±4) and (±2,0), with values −48 and 8. The interior critical point (0,0) gives 0. Thus the global minimum is −48.

The earlier answer −8 (option c) was graded Correct and agrees with MA's worked solution. There are no interior critical points since f_y=−4. question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)=10+x+y$ given that ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical points in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=2\lambda x \\ 1=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{2\lambda } \\ y=\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
y=x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),\,(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ | $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $10+\sqrt{2}$ | $10-\sqrt{2}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),$ and its minimum value is $10-\sqrt{2}.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function f(x,y)=10+x+y given that x2+y2≤1.

a
 10
b
 10−3
c
 10+2
d
 10
e
 10−2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving ∇f=0, as follows:

⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=⟨0,0⟩⟨1,1⟩=⟨0,0⟩

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical points in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of f(x,y) subject to the constraint g(x,y)=x2+y2=1.

Since f(x,y) is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, f(x,y) reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint.

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y)g(x,y)=1

We start by solving the first equation:

∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y)⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=λ⟨gx(x,y),gy(x,y)⟩⟨1,1⟩=λ⟨2x,2y⟩

Notice that we cannot have λ=0 since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming λ≠0, we have the following:

{1=2λx1=2λy⇒{x=12λy=12λ⇒x=y

Substituting y=x into the condition g(x,y)=1, we get

x2+y2=1x2+x2=12x2=1x2=12x=±12.

As a result, y=x=±12.

Therefore, f has possible extreme values at the points

(22,22),(−22,−22).

We evaluate f at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

(x,y) (22,22) (−22,−22)
f(x,y) 10+2 10−2

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at (−22,−22), and its minimum value is 10−2.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical points in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=1
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=2\lambda x \\ 1=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{2\lambda } \\ y=\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
y=x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),\,(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ | $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $10+\sqrt{2}$ | $10-\sqrt{2}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),$ and its minimum value is $10-\sqrt{2}.$

\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=2\lambda x \\ 1=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{1}{2\lambda } \\ y=\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=x$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{x}^{2} & =1 \\ 2{x}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
y=x=\pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),\,(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ | $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $10+\sqrt{2}$ | $10-\sqrt{2}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}),$ and its minimum value is $10-\sqrt{2}.$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: A rectangular box without a lid has a surface area of $48{\text{ cm}}^{2}.$ Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum possible volume of the box.
question.worked_solution:
Let $x,y$, and $z$ be the box's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to maximize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xyz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
2xz+2yz+xy=48.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=2xz+2yz+xy.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=48
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2z+y,2z+x,2x+2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}yz=\lambda (2z+y) \\ xz=\lambda (2z+x) \\ xy=\lambda (2x+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}xyz=\lambda x(2z+y) \\ xyz=\lambda y(2z+x) \\ xyz=\lambda z(2x+2y)\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $xyz=0,$ which contradicts the constraints. Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2z+y) & =y(2z+x) \\ 2xz+xy & =2yz+xy \\ xz & =yz\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z\ne 0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $x=y=2z.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2xz+2yz+xy & =48 \\ 4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =48 \\ 12{z}^{2} & =48 \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the maximum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(4,4,2),$ and the maximum value is 

$$
f(4,4,2)=4\cdot 4\cdot 2=32\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2,5.5) & =2\cdot 2\cdot 5.5 \\  & =22 \\  & <f(4,4,2).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

A rectangular box without a lid has a surface area of 48 cm2. Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum possible volume of the box.

a
 32 cm3
b
 24 cm3
c
 48 cm3
d
 54 cm3
e
 36 cm3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let x,y, and z be the box's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to maximize the function f(x,y,z)=xyz, subject to the constraint 2xz+2yz+xy=48.

Note that we also have the constraints x>0,y>0,z>0.

Let g(x,y,z)=2xz+2yz+xy. Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system: ∇f(x,y,z)=λ∇g(x,y,z),g(x,y,z)=48

We start by solving the first equation:

∇f(x,y,z)=λ∇g(x,y,z)⟨fx(x,y,z),fy(x,y,z),fz(x,y,z)⟩=λ⟨gx(x,y,z),gy(x,y,z),gz(x,y,z)⟩⟨yz,xz,xy⟩=λ⟨2z+y,2z+x,2x+2y⟩

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

{yz=λ(2z+y)xz=λ(2z+x)xy=λ(2x+2y)

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by x,y, and z respectively, we get the following:

{xyz=λx(2z+y)xyz=λy(2z+x)xyz=λz(2x+2y)

We cannot have λ=0 since this would give xyz=0, which contradicts the constraints. Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have x(2z+y)=y(2z+x)2xz+xy=2yz+xyxz=yz

Since z≠0, we can conclude that x=y.

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that x=y=2z. So, using the constraint equation, we get 2xz+2yz+xy=484z2+4z2+4z2=4812z2=48z=2.

Therefore, the maximum value of f is reached at the point (4,4,2), and the maximum value is

f(4,4,2)=4⋅4⋅2=32cm3.

Note: It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, f(2,2,5.5)=2⋅2⋅5.5=22<f(4,4,2).

solution.reasoning: Let x,y be the base dimensions and h the height. Maximize V=xyh subject to xy+2xh+2yh=48. The Lagrange equations give x=y=2h, hence 12h²=48, so h=2 and x=y=4 cm. Thus V=32 cm³. This is the global maximum: AM–GM gives (xy)(2xh)(2yh)≤16³, so 4V²≤4096 and V≤32. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was supplied.

$$

Question 3
?

Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, determine the maximum product of three positive numbers given that the sum of their squares is 108.

a
216
b
1052
c
255
d
256
e
125
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let x, y, and z be three positive numbers. We wish to maximize the function f(x,y,z)=xyz, subject to the constraint x2+y2+z2=108.

Note that we also have the constraints x>0,y>0,z>0.

Let g(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2. Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system: ∇f(x,y,z)=λ∇g(x,y,z),g(x,y,z)=108

We start by solving the first equation: ∇f(x,y,z)=λ∇g(x,y,z)⟨fx(x,y,z),fy(x,y,z),fz(x,y,z)⟩=λ⟨gx(x,y,z),gy(x,y,z),gz(x,y,z)⟩⟨yz,xz,xy⟩=λ⟨2x,2y,2z⟩

Therefore, we have the following system of equations: {yz=2λxxz=2λyxy=2λz

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by x,y, and z respectively, we get the following: {xyz=2λx2xyz=2λy2xyz=2λz2

This gives x=y=z.

Now, using the constraint equation, we get x2+y2+z2=108x2+x2+x2=1083x2=108x2=36x=6.

Therefore, the maximum value of f is reached at the point (6,6,6), and the maximum value is f(6,6,6)=6⋅6⋅6=216.

Note: It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the maximum (and not the minimum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, f(10,2,2)=10⋅2⋅2=40<f(6,6,6).

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}$ given that $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 16.$ 

*Hint: The critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region $4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}<16$ is $(0,0).$*
question.worked_solution:
We are given that the critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region's interior is $(0,0).$

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=16
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4x,-6y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨8x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}4x=8\lambda x \\ -6y=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(1-2\lambda )=0 \\ y(3+\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,y=\pm 4.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,\pm 4).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=16$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2} & =16\,⇒\,x=\pm 2,\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm 2,0).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm 4),\,(\pm 2,0),\,(0,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,\pm 4)$ | $(\pm 2,0)$ | $(0,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $-48$ | $8$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,\pm 4),$ and its minimum value is $-48.$

$$

$$

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-4⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{2}y=-2\,⇒\,y=-4.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+(-4)^{2}=4\,⇒\,{x}^{2}=-6\end{aligned}
$$

which has no solutions.

$$
(0,\pm 2).

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,2)$ | $(0,-2)$ |

\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-4⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2x=4\lambda x \\ -4=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(1-2\lambda )=0 \\ \lambda y=-2\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4\,⇒\,y=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,\pm 2).$

- Assuming $\lambda =\frac{1}{2}$ in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies 

$$
\frac{1}{2}y=-2\,⇒\,y=-4.
$$

 
Then, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+(-4)^{2}=4\,⇒\,{x}^{2}=-6\end{aligned}
$$

which has no solutions.

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm 2).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,2)$ | $(0,-2)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $-8$ | $8$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,2),$ and its minimum value is $-8.$

Question 5
?

Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function f(x,y)=x2−4y given that 2x2+y2≤4.

a
−10
b
−5
c
−8
d
1
e
4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving ∇f=0, as follows:

⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=⟨0,0⟩⟨2x,−4⟩=⟨0,0⟩

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of f(x,y) subject to the constraint g(x,y)=2x2+y2=4.

Since f(x,y) is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, f(x,y) reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint.

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y),g(x,y)=4

We start by solving the first equation:

∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y)⟨fx(x,y),fy(x,y)⟩=λ⟨gx(x,y),gy(x,y)⟩⟨2x,−4⟩=λ⟨4x,2y⟩

Therefore, we have the following:

{2x=4λx−4=2λy⇒{x(1−2λ)=0λy=−2

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

  • Assuming x=0 in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition g(x,y)=4 implies 2(0)2+y2=4⇒y=±2. This gives the critical points (0,±2).

  • Assuming λ=12 in the first equation of the system, the second equation of the system implies 12y=−2⇒y=−4. Then, the constraint condition g(x,y)=4 implies 2x2+(−4)2=4⇒x2=−6 which has no solutions.

Therefore, f has possible extreme values at the points (0,±2).

We evaluate f at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

(x,y) (0,2) (0,−2)
f(x,y) −8 8

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at (0,2), and its minimum value is −8.

solution.reasoning: There are no interior critical points because f_y=−4. On 2x²+y²=4, the Lagrange equations are 2x=4λx and −4=2λy. If x≠0, then λ=1/2 and y=−4, which violates the constraint. Thus x=0 and y=±2, giving f=−8 and 8. The minimum is −8 at (0,2). No Math Academy answer-key evidence was supplied.

To find the coordinates of the point, we inspect its position along the $x$- and $y$-axes.

* The point is $2$ units to the *left* of the origin, in the *negative* direction of the $x$-axis. So, its $x$-coordinate is $-2.$

* The point is $3$ units *above* the origin, in the *positive* direction of the $y$-axis. So, its $y$-coordinate is $3.$

Therefore, the coordinates of our point are $(-2,3).$

questions.worked_solution:
We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form 

$$
y=mx+b.
$$

As we found previously, the slope is $m=-\frac{1}{3}.$

Substituting $m=-\frac{1}{3}$ into the slope-intercept form above, we get

$$
y=-\frac{1}{3}x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(4,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+b \\ 1 & =-(\frac{1}{3})(4)+b \\ 1 & =-\frac{4}{3}+b \\ 1+\frac{4}{3} & =b \\ b & =\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is 

$$
y=-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3}.
$$

Previously, we found that $\overset{↔}{AB}$ has equation

$$
y=-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3}.
$$

At the $x$-intercept, the $y$-coordinate is equal to $0.$ So, we can substitute $y=0$ into the equation and then solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3} \\ 0 & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3} \\ 0 & =-x+7 \\ x & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$-intercept is $x=7.$ The coordinates of the $x$-intercept are $(7,0).$

questions.worked_solution:
Our goal is to write the equation in the form 

$$
ax+by=c,
$$

where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors and $a\ge 0.$

We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3} \\ \frac{1}{3}x+y & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x+3y & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So, we are done!

The standard form of the line is 

$$
x+3y=7.
$$

$$
m=-\frac{1}{3}.

So, we want a line with the slope $m=-\frac{1}{3}$ that passes through the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(3,-2).$ 

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =-\frac{1}{3}\cdot (x-3) \\ y+2 & =-\frac{1}{3}x+1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{m}_{1}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{3})}=3.
$$

So, our perpendicular line has the slope ${m}_{1}=3$ and passes through the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,8).$ 

Finally, using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}_{1}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-8 & =3(x-2) \\ y-8 & =3x-6 \\ y & =3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form 

$$
y=mx+b.
$$

As we found previously, the slope is $m=-\frac{1}{3}.$

Substituting $m=-\frac{1}{3}$ into the slope-intercept form above, we get

$$
y=-\frac{1}{3}x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(4,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+b \\ 1 & =-(\frac{1}{3})(4)+b \\ 1 & =-\frac{4}{3}+b \\ 1+\frac{4}{3} & =b \\ b & =\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is 

$$
y=-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{7}{3}.
$$

Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other. Therefore, since $\overset{↔}{AB}$ has the slope $m=-\frac{1}{3},$ our perpendicular line must have a slope of 

$$
{m}_{1}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{3})}=3.
$$

So, our perpendicular line has the slope ${m}_{1}=3$ and passes through the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(2,8).$ 

Finally, using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}_{1}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-8 & =3(x-2) \\ y-8 & =3x-6 \\ y & =3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{e}^{y},x=2t$ and $y={t}^{2},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14213676/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2t){e}^{{t}^{2}}=4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2t)^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}=4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =8t{e}^{{t}^{2}}+8{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{2}} \\  & =8t(1+{t}^{2}){e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=y+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,x=s$ and $y=2s,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14213676/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+yx$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}+y)$ and $y=\frac{1}{x},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x+1}$ and $y={x}^{3},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

5.Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case?

If f(x,y)=yx+1 and y=x3, compute dfdx.

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14213676/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2t){e}^{{t}^{2}}=4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2t)^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}=4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =8t{e}^{{t}^{2}}+8{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{2}} \\  & =8t(1+{t}^{2}){e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=x2ey,x=2t and y=t2, compute dfdt.

a
 2t2(1+t2)et2
b
4t(1+2t)et2
c
8t(1+t2)et2
d
4t(2+t)et2
e
8t3(2+t)et2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2xey,∂f∂y=x2ey

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=2(2t)et2=4tet2,∂f∂y=(2t)2et2=4t2et2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=2,dydt=2t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=4tet2⋅2+4t2et2⋅2t=8tet2+8t3et2=8t(1+t2)et2.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14213676/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: If $f(x,y)=y+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,x=s$ and $y=2s,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14213676/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2

If f(x,y)=y+xln⁡y,x=s and y=2s, compute dfds.

a
3+ln⁡2s
b
34+ln⁡2s
c
32+ln⁡2s
d
3ln⁡2s
e
ln⁡2s
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=ln⁡y,∂f∂y=1+xy

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get

∂f∂x=ln⁡2s,∂f∂y=1+s2s=32.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

dxds=1,dyds=2.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds=ln⁡2s⋅1+32⋅2=3+ln⁡2s.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x+y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =2x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y),\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}), \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-2x)\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =(\frac{1-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{{x}^{3}+1}{x}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

If f(x,y)=cos⁡(x2+y) and y=1x, compute dfdx.

a
(1−2x3x2)sin⁡(x3+1x)
b
(2x2+1x)sin⁡(x3+1x)
c
(1+4x2)cos⁡(x2−1x)
d
(1−3x3)sin⁡(x2+1x2)
e
(1−4x3x)cos⁡(x3+1x2)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows: dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−2xsin⁡(x2+y),∂f∂y=−sin⁡(x2+y)

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=−2xsin⁡(x2+1x),∂f∂y=−sin⁡(x2+1x).

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=−1x2.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=−2xsin⁡(x2+1x)+(−sin⁡(x2+1x))⋅(−1x2)=(1x2−2x)sin⁡(x2+1x)=(1−2x3x2)sin⁡(x3+1x).

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: If $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{x+1}$ and $y={x}^{3},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}.$
question.worked_solution:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y=y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-\frac{y}{(x+1)^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{x+1}\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{x+1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}(x+1)-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}(2x+3)}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

If f(x,y)=yx+1 and y=x3, compute dfdx.

a
x2(3x2−1)(x+1)2
b
4x2(x−6)x+1
c
x(3x+4)(x+1)2
d
x2(2x+3)(x+1)2
e
x(4x−3)x+1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) in the case where y=y(x) can be expressed as follows: dfdx=∂f∂x+∂f∂y⋅dydx

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y: ∂f∂x=−y(x+1)2,∂f∂y=1x+1

Writing the above results in terms of x, we get ∂f∂x=−x3(x+1)2,∂f∂y=1x+1.

Next, we take the derivative y with respect to x, and we get dydx=3x2.

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get dfdx=−x3(x+1)2+1x+1⋅3x2=3x2x+1−x3(x+1)2=3x2(x+1)−x3(x+1)2=3x3+3x2−x3(x+1)2=x2(2x+3)(x+1)2.

The Incorrect grade applies to the actually submitted option b, 3/4+\ln(2s), which differs from the correct derivative by 9/4; it does not contradict the earlier answer.

Substituting y=\sin x gives f(x)=x^2+x\sin x. Differentiating gives 2x+\sin x+x\cos x, confirming the earlier option e. Math Academy graded that exact submission Correct, and its worked solution states the same derivative.

For x\ne0, differentiating cos(x^2+1/x) gives (1/x^2-2x)\sin(x^2+1/x), equivalent to option a. The captured worked solution confirms this earlier answer. The Incorrect grade applies to the actually submitted option b, not the earlier recommended option a, and is mathematically consistent.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: If $f(x,y)={x}^{2}{e}^{y},x=2t$ and $y={t}^{2},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}.$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14213676/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2t){e}^{{t}^{2}}=4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2t)^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}=4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =8t{e}^{{t}^{2}}+8{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{2}} \\  & =8t(1+{t}^{2}){e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=x2ey,x=2t and y=t2, compute dfdt.

a
 2t2(1+t2)et2
b
4t(1+2t)et2
c
8t(1+t2)et2
d
4t(2+t)et2
e
8t3(2+t)et2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2xey,∂f∂y=x2ey

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=2(2t)et2=4tet2,∂f∂y=(2t)2et2=4t2et2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=2,dydt=2t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=4tet2⋅2+4t2et2⋅2t=8tet2+8t3et2=8t(1+t2)et2.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14213676/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2t){e}^{{t}^{2}}=4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2t)^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}=4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =8t{e}^{{t}^{2}}+8{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{2}} \\  & =8t(1+{t}^{2}){e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=x2ey,x=2t and y=t2, compute dfdt.

a
 2t2(1+t2)et2
b
4t(1+2t)et2
c
8t(1+t2)et2
d
4t(2+t)et2
e
8t3(2+t)et2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2xey,∂f∂y=x2ey

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=2(2t)et2=4tet2,∂f∂y=(2t)2et2=4t2et2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=2,dydt=2t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=4tet2⋅2+4t2et2⋅2t=8tet2+8t3et2=8t(1+t2)et2.

solution.reasoning: Substituting gives f(t)=4t^2e^{t^2}. The product and chain rules give df/dt=8te^{t^2}+8t^3e^{t^2}=8t(1+t^2)e^{t^2}, matching option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14213676/assets/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{e}^{y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}={x}^{2}{e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2(2t){e}^{{t}^{2}}=4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(2t)^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}=4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4t{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+4{t}^{2}{e}^{{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t \\  & =8t{e}^{{t}^{2}}+8{t}^{3}{e}^{{t}^{2}} \\  & =8t(1+{t}^{2}){e}^{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=x2ey,x=2t and y=t2, compute dfdt.

a
 2t2(1+t2)et2
b
4t(1+2t)et2
c
8t(1+t2)et2
d
4t(2+t)et2
e
8t3(2+t)et2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable t, where x=x(t) and y=y(t), can be expressed as follows:

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=2xey,∂f∂y=x2ey

Writing the above results in terms of t, we get

∂f∂x=2(2t)et2=4tet2,∂f∂y=(2t)2et2=4t2et2.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to t, and we get

dxdt=2,dydt=2t.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

dfdt=∂f∂x⋅dxdt+∂f∂y⋅dydt=4tet2⋅2+4t2et2⋅2t=8tet2+8t3et2=8t(1+t2)et2.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: If $f(x,y)=y+x\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,x=s$ and $y=2s,$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}.$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14213676/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=y+xln⁡y,x=s and y=2s, compute dfds.

a
3+ln⁡2s
b
34+ln⁡2s
c
32+ln⁡2s
d
3ln⁡2s
e
ln⁡2s
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule for a multivariable function f(x,y) with one independent variable s, where x=x(s) and y=y(s), can be expressed as follows:

dfds=∂f∂x⋅dxds+∂f∂y⋅dyds

First, we find the partial derivatives of f with respect to x and y:

∂f∂x=ln⁡y,∂f∂y=1+xy

Writing the above results in terms of s, we get

∂f∂x=ln⁡2s,∂f∂y=1+s2s=32.

Next, we take the derivatives of x and y with respect to s, and we get

dxds=1,dyds=2.

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14213676/assets/7e5b5001794ecdf2c9b9e9102f334a63d2c59bc6f7511c2eb7fa358fc94cb0c5.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x=x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=1+\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =1+\frac{s}{2s}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}=1,\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}s} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}s}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}s} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2s\cdot 1+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 2 \\  & =3+\operatorname{ln}⁡2s.\end{aligned}
$$
